title: Find a spring constant from launch heights

stimulus.title: A vertical spring launcher
stimulus.text: A toy launcher holds a vertical spring with a light platform on top. A student places a 0.050 kg ball on the platform, pushes it down to compress the spring by x, and releases it. The ball flies straight up and reaches a greatest height h above its launch point (its position with the spring compressed). The student wants to determine the spring constant k. Air resistance is negligible.

table.caption: Compression and greatest height (mean of three trials each)

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe a procedure the student could use to collect the data in the table. Name each quantity measured and the equipment used to measure it, and describe what the student could do to reduce experimental uncertainty.

rubric.point: Measures the compression x with a ruler or meterstick (the distance the platform moves down).
accept: mark the platform's relaxed and compressed positions

rubric.point: Measures the greatest height h with a meterstick (or video against a scale) from the launch point.
accept: meterstick held vertically next to the flight
slow-motion video with a meterstick in view

rubric.point: Reduces uncertainty: repeats each compression several times and averages, and/or uses a range of at least five different compressions.
accept: several values of x spread over the range

parts.sample: Clamp a meterstick vertically beside the launcher. Note the platform's height with the spring relaxed, push the ball down by a measured x (read on the meterstick or a ruler), and release. Read the highest point of the ball on the meterstick (a phone video in slow motion makes this easier) and subtract the launch position to get h. Do three trials at each compression and average them, and repeat for at least five compressions from 0.010 m to 0.050 m.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Indicate what quantities the student should graph to produce a straight line that could be used to determine k, and explain how k could be found from the graph.

rubric.point: Graph h on the vertical axis against x² on the horizontal axis (or the reverse).
States that the slope is k/(2mg), so k = 2mg × slope (or the inverse relation if the axes are swapped), from ½kx² = mgh.

parts.sample: For the ball-spring-Earth system, mechanical energy is constant: ½kx² = mgh, so h = (k/(2mg))x². A graph of h against x² is a straight line through the origin with slope k/(2mg), so k = 2mg × slope.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: On the grid, plot the data points for the quantities you indicated in part (b). Clearly scale and label the axes, including units. Draw a straight line that best represents the data.

rubric.point: Axes labeled with quantities and units (h in m; x² in m²).
Linear scales that use most of the grid, and the five points plotted correctly (x² = 1.0, 4.0, 9.0, 16, 25 × 10⁻⁴ m²).
accept: points within one small square of the correct positions

rubric.point: A single straight best-fit line (not connecting the dots), passing close to the origin.
accept: ruled line with points on both sides

parts.sample: Horizontal axis x² (× 10⁻⁴ m²) from 0 to 25; vertical axis h (m) from 0 to 0.70. The points (1.0, 0.027), (4.0, 0.098), (9.0, 0.236), (16, 0.401), (25, 0.645) lie close to a straight line through the origin, drawn with a ruler as a best fit.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Calculate the spring constant k using your best-fit line. Use g = 9.8 m/s².

rubric.point: Uses the slope of the best-fit line (not a single data point), about 257 m⁻¹ (accept 236 to 277).
accept: slope from two points on the line, far apart

rubric.point: Correct k = 2mg × slope, about 252 N/m (accept 220 to 280 N/m, consistent with the student's slope), with units.

parts.sample: Two points on the best-fit line, (0, 0) and (25 × 10⁻⁴ m², 0.645 m), give a slope of about 258 m⁻¹ (m per m²). Then k = 2mg × slope = 2(0.050 kg)(9.8 m/s²)(258 m⁻¹) ≈ 2.5 × 10² N/m.
